buildUp: You need a steady beat, so the heart of the watch is a balance wheel with a hairspring that swings at a fixed rate, about four times a second.

Something has to keep the balance swinging against friction and count its swings, so an escapement of pallet fork and escape wheel gives it a nudge and lets the gears move on exactly one step per swing.
That needs a source of energy for days, so a long mainspring is coiled in a barrel, and a gear train steps its slow, strong turning up to the fast, gentle turning the escapement needs.
To read the time, wheels in the train are chosen to turn once a minute and once an hour, with extra gearing for the hour hand, and the hands sit on top of a dial behind a sapphire crystal.
Friction would waste the tiny energy budget and wear the pivots, so the fast-moving shafts run in synthetic ruby jewels, held between a main plate and bridges.

Finally, to save the wearer from winding it each day, a weighted rotor swings with every movement of the wrist and winds the mainspring automatically, and the case seals everything against water and dust.
firstPrinciples.coreIdea: Let a tiny spring-loaded wheel swing back and forth at a fixed rate, and let it release the stored energy of a mainspring one small step per swing. The swinging balance is the clock; the escapement is a gate that lets the gears advance only when the balance says so, and gives it a tiny push each time to keep it swinging. Gears then turn that count of ticks into the movement of the hands.

hardParts.title: A hairspring as steady as a clock must be
hardParts.why: The hairspring's stiffness sets the rate of the whole watch, yet this coil only a few hundredths of a millimetre thick must stay the same through hot and cold days and resist magnetism. It must also breathe evenly in and out so the balance stays centred. Getting the alloy, the coil shape and the attachment points right is the hardest part of making a watch accurate.

hardParts.title: An escapement that pushes without disturbing
hardParts.why: The escapement has to unlock the gear train, give the balance a small push and lock again, eight times a second, about 690,000 times a day. Every contact steals a little energy and nudges the balance's timing, so the pallet fork and escape wheel teeth are shaped to touch as briefly and lightly as possible, and are lubricated with tiny drops of special oil.

hardParts.title: Machining to a few microns
hardParts.why: Wheels a few tenths of a millimetre thick, pivots about a tenth of a millimetre across and plates machined to within a few microns must all line up so that each shaft turns freely without wobbling. Any burr, dust or slightly misplaced hole costs energy and timekeeping, and the parts are far too small to adjust by hand at full size.

principles.explanation: The balance wheel swings at a rate set by its weight and its hairspring's stiffness, not by how far it swings, so the watch keeps time as the mainspring runs down. A child on a swing goes back and forth at nearly the same rate whether pushed high or low. The balance wheel and hairspring work the same way: the spring pulls the wheel back towards the middle, the wheel overshoots, and the spring pulls it back again. How often it swings is set by how heavy the wheel's rim is and how stiff the spring is. Here it swings four times a second, giving eight ticks.
principles.title: Oscillators keep their own time

principles.explanation: The watch's gears turn the mainspring's slow, forceful pull into the fast, gentle motion the escapement needs, and count time for the hands along the way. When a big wheel drives a small one, the small one turns faster but with less force; the product of the two stays almost the same. The mainspring's barrel turns only a few times a day with great force, and a chain of wheels multiplies that speed several thousand times by the time it reaches the escape wheel, leaving only a whisper of force. The same gears count, too: if the fourth wheel turns once a minute, it can carry the seconds hand.
principles.title: Gears trade force for speed

principles.explanation: The coiled mainspring is the watch's only store of energy, and it holds well under a joule, so everything in the watch must waste almost nothing. Bending or coiling springy steel stores energy in its stretched atomic bonds, and it gives that energy back as it uncoils. A mainspring about half a metre long, wound tightly into a drum, holds roughly what it takes to lift an apple a few tens of centimetres. Spread over about 48 hours, that's only a few millionths of a watt.
principles.title: A spring is a battery for motion

principles.explanation: There are 86,400 seconds in a day, so an error of 10 seconds a day means the balance must keep its rate to about one part in 10,000. Anything that changes the spring's stiffness or the wheel's size by that much shows up on the dial: warmth makes metal expand and most metal springs go softer, a magnet can make coils stick together, and gravity pulls the balance slightly differently depending on how the watch is held. Much of watchmaking is fighting these tiny effects.
principles.title: Small errors add up fast

firstPrinciples.problem: Keep time to within a few seconds a day, on a wrist that swings, bumps and changes temperature, with no battery and nothing to plug in. You need something that repeats at a perfectly steady rate, a store of energy to keep it going for days, and a way to count its beats and show them as hours and minutes. All of it has to fit in a space a few centimetres across and run for years with almost no friction.

questions.answer: A weaker push makes the balance swing through a smaller arc, but a spring-and-wheel oscillator takes nearly the same time per swing whatever its size. So the rate barely changes, much as a swing keeps the same rhythm whether pushed high or low.
questions.question: As the mainspring runs down and pushes more weakly, why doesn't the watch slow down?

questions.answer: The escapement lets the gear train advance only when the balance swings past the pallet fork, then locks it again. Each release moves the seconds hand one small step, eight times a second.
questions.question: Why does the watch tick rather than move smoothly?

questions.answer: Ruby is extremely hard and can be made very smooth, so a steel pivot turning in it has little friction and almost no wear over years. With energy measured in millionths of a watt, every bit of friction saved matters.
questions.question: Why use ruby for bearings instead of polished steel?

firstPrinciples.xFactor: A mechanical watch runs for two days on about as much energy as it takes to lift an apple off a table, and stays accurate to roughly one part in 10,000. The insight that makes it possible is to separate the jobs: the spring only supplies energy, the balance only keeps time, and the escapement links them so that the variable push of the spring barely disturbs the steady swing of the balance.

name: Mechanical Watch
overview:
A mechanical watch keeps time with springs and gears and no battery. Everything is driven by one coiled mainspring. In an automatic watch like this one, a weighted rotor swings as you move your wrist and winds the spring for you; you can also wind it with the crown.

The mainspring unwinds through a gear train: a series of wheels, each turning faster than the last, that end at the escapement. On its own the spring would let go in seconds. The escapement makes it go slowly: an escape wheel is locked and released one tooth at a time by the pallet fork, which is rocked back and forth by the balance wheel. That release is the tick you hear.

The balance wheel and its hairspring are the actual timekeeper. Like a pendulum, they swing back and forth at a steady rate, here four times a second, and each swing in either direction lets the gear train advance one step: eight ticks a second. Gears off the train turn the minute hand once an hour and the hour hand once every twelve hours. Synthetic ruby jewels serve as nearly frictionless bearings.

parts.description: Synthetic sapphire window: almost as hard as diamond, so it shrugs off scratches.

details.didYouKnow: Synthetic sapphire is chemically the same stuff as ruby. The only difference is a trace of chromium, which turns it red, and that is exactly what the jewel bearings inside are made of.
details.howItWorks: The crystal is the clear front window that keeps fingers, dust and water off the hands. It is pressed into the bezel with a thin gasket around its edge, so it seals as well as protects. An anti-reflective coating on one or both faces stops glare from hiding the dial.
keyNumbers: Hardness: 9 on the Mohs scale (diamond is 10)
details.madeOf: Synthetic sapphire, which is crystallised aluminium oxide grown in a furnace and then sliced, ground and polished with diamond tools. Nothing softer than diamond can cut it, which is why it stays clear for decades.

parts.name: Sapphire crystal

parts.description: Polished ring that clamps the crystal onto the case.

details.didYouKnow: On dive watches the bezel rotates one way only and carries a minute scale, so a diver can time their air supply without any risk of a bump making the dive look shorter.
details.howItWorks: The bezel is the ring around the crystal that holds it down against the case. On a dress watch like this one it is usually a tight press fit, snapped on with a hand press so the crystal and its gasket are squeezed into a watertight seal. Its polished slopes also frame the dial and catch the light.
keyNumbers: Outer diameter: about 40 mm, matching the case
Press-fit force: up to a few hundred newtons
Polishing: often several stages from coarse to mirror
details.madeOf: Usually the same 316L stainless steel as the case, machined on a CNC lathe and then polished by hand on buffing wheels so it matches the case finish.

parts.name: Bezel

parts.description: Stainless-steel ring that the movement sits in; the lugs for the strap are part of it.

details.didYouKnow: A 100 m water-resistance rating is a pressure test in a lab, not a promise you can dive to 100 m. Swinging your arm through water can briefly push the pressure well above the static figure.
details.howItWorks: The case middle is the main body of the watch. The movement sits inside it on a spacer ring, the bezel and crystal close the front, the case back screws into the rear, and the crown passes through a sealed tube in its side. Because the lugs are part of the same piece, every pull on the strap is taken by this one solid block of steel.
keyNumbers: Thickness: typically about 10 to 13 mm with crystal and back
Water resistance: typically 50 to 100 m rated
details.madeOf: Most steel watches use 316L stainless steel, an alloy with chromium, nickel and molybdenum that resists sweat and seawater. The case is usually forged or stamped roughly to shape, then CNC machined and polished.

parts.name: Case

parts.description: Horn that holds one end of a spring bar.

details.didYouKnow: Lug-to-lug length often matters more than case diameter for comfort: if the lugs overhang the edges of your wrist, even a small watch can look and feel too big.
details.howItWorks: Each lug is a horn sticking out from the case, and each pair of lugs has small holes drilled on their inner faces. The spring bar's tips snap into those holes, so the strap is held between the lugs. Their length and curve decide how well the watch hugs your wrist.
keyNumbers: Gap between lugs: typically about 20 mm on a 40 mm watch
Lug-to-lug length: usually about 46 to 50 mm
details.madeOf: The lugs are machined out of the same stainless steel block as the case, so there are no joints to loosen or corrode.

parts.name: Lug

parts.description: Horn that holds one end of a spring bar.

details.didYouKnow: Early wristwatches were often converted pocket watches with wire loops soldered on for a strap. Built-in lugs became standard as wristwatches took over in the early twentieth century.
details.howItWorks: This lug pairs with its neighbour to grip a spring bar from both ends, which in turn carries one half of the strap. The steel has to cope with sudden tugs, such as catching the strap on a door handle, without bending. Some watches drill the holes right through the lug so a strap can be changed with a pin pushed from outside.
keyNumbers: Usual lug widths: about 18, 20 or 22 mm
Lugs per watch: 4, two at each end
details.madeOf: Solid stainless steel, part of the one-piece case, usually given the same brushed or polished finish so the lines flow from case to strap.

parts.name: Lug

parts.description: Spring-loaded pin that snaps between the lugs to hold the strap.

details.didYouKnow: The little shoulder near each end of a spring bar is there for a forked tool to catch on, which is how a watchmaker compresses it in seconds.
details.howItWorks: A spring bar is a little tube with a pin poking out of each end and a coil spring inside pushing them apart. You squeeze the pins in, slide the bar between the lugs, and let them pop out into the lug holes. The strap's end loop wraps around the bar, so it carries all the strap's load.
keyNumbers: Tube diameter: typically about 1.5 to 1.8 mm
Length: matches the lug gap, often 20 mm
details.madeOf: Stainless steel tube with hardened steel pins and a tiny steel spring, chosen so the bar stays strong and springy without rusting from sweat.

parts.name: Spring bar

parts.description: One half of the strap.

details.didYouKnow: Water and sweat are leather's enemies, which is why a leather strap usually wears out long before the watch needs its first service.
details.howItWorks: The strap comes in two halves: one carries the buckle and the other the holes. Each end loops around a spring bar between the lugs. Leather is padded and stitched in layers so it flexes around the wrist but does not stretch out of shape.
keyNumbers: Width at the lugs: about 20 mm
Taper at the buckle: often about 16 to 18 mm
Typical lengths: roughly 75 mm and 115 mm halves
details.madeOf: Tanned calf leather is the classic choice, often with a softer lining and a filler layer glued and stitched together. Tanning makes the hide flexible and stops it rotting.

parts.name: Leather strap

parts.description: Knob for winding the mainspring by hand and, pulled out, setting the time.

details.didYouKnow: It is called the crown because on pocket watches it sat on top of the case at 12 o'clock, like a crown on a head.
details.howItWorks: Pushed in, turning the crown winds the mainspring through the keyless works inside the movement. Pulled out one click, it usually sets the date; pulled out fully, it moves the hands and on many movements stops the balance so you can set the seconds exactly. Rubber seals inside the crown and its tube keep water out at every position.
keyNumbers: Hand winding from empty: roughly 30 to 40 turns
details.madeOf: Stainless steel, machined and given a grippy knurled edge, with one or more rubber O-rings inside to seal against the case tube.

parts.name: Crown

parts.description: Thin shaft linking the crown to the winding and setting gears inside the movement.

details.didYouKnow: When a watch is cased, the watchmaker trims the stem to length by hand so the crown sits snugly against the case without pressing on the movement.
details.howItWorks: The stem runs from the crown through the case into the movement. A square section along it drives a sliding clutch wheel, which a lever shifts between the winding gears and the hand-setting gears as you pull the crown in and out. Pressing a small release lever lets the stem slide out, which is how a watchmaker lifts the movement from the case.
keyNumbers: Length: roughly 10 to 15 mm, cut to fit the case
details.madeOf: Hardened and tempered carbon or stainless steel, threaded at the outer end to screw into the crown. It must be stiff enough not to twist under winding torque.

parts.name: Winding stem

parts.description: Rubber O-ring that keeps water and dust out.

details.didYouKnow: Rubber gaskets slowly harden with age, which is why an old watch that was once water-resistant should be pressure tested before you swim in it.
details.howItWorks: The gasket is a ring of rubber sitting in a groove between the case middle and the case back. Screwing the back down squeezes it, so it fills every tiny gap and blocks water, dust and moisture. A thin smear of silicone grease helps it seal and stops it drying out.
keyNumbers: Replacement: usually at every service, roughly every 5 years
details.madeOf: Usually nitrile rubber or another synthetic rubber, which stays springy for years and does not swell in sweat or skin oils.

parts.name: Case-back gasket

parts.description: Screw-down steel back that seals the case.

details.didYouKnow: Many automatic watches swap the steel back for one with a sapphire window, so you can watch the rotor swing and the balance tick.
details.howItWorks: The case back closes the rear of the case. It screws onto a fine thread in the case middle, crushing the gasket to make the seal. Notches around its edge let a watchmaker's case wrench grip it to open the watch for service.
keyNumbers: Thread pitch: fine, typically well under 1 mm
details.madeOf: Stainless steel, machined and threaded, often with engraving or stamped markings such as the reference number and water rating.

parts.name: Case back

parts.description: Sweeps round in tiny steps, one for every tick of the escapement.

details.didYouKnow: That smooth sweep is how people tell a mechanical watch from a quartz one at a glance, since most quartz seconds hands jump just once a second.
details.howItWorks: The seconds hand is pressed onto the arbor of the fourth wheel, which turns once a minute. Because the escapement releases the train in small jumps, the hand moves in tiny steps rather than a true glide. A short tail on the back balances its weight so it does not drag on the gears.
keyNumbers: Steps per second: 8 at 28,800 vibrations per hour
details.madeOf: Thin brass or steel, stamped and painted or lacquered, kept extremely light so it does not upset the train or shake loose in a knock.

parts.name: Seconds hand

parts.description: Driven once round per hour by the centre wheel.

details.didYouKnow: Hands are simply pushed onto their tubes, so fitting them so they line up exactly at 12 o'clock is a delicate job done under magnification.
details.howItWorks: The minute hand sits on the cannon pinion, a tube that grips the centre wheel arbor by friction. When the watch runs, friction carries the hand round once an hour. When you set the time, the crown turns the cannon pinion and it simply slips on the arbor, so the train and balance are not dragged backwards.
keyNumbers: Turns: once per hour, 24 times a day
Length: about the radius of the minute track, roughly 15 to 18 mm here
details.madeOf: Stamped or machined steel or brass, often polished or plated and sometimes filled with luminous paint.

parts.name: Minute hand

parts.description: Geared down twelve to one from the minute hand.

details.didYouKnow: The hour wheel only turns twice a day, so its teeth barely wear, but it is what triggers the date change at midnight.
details.howItWorks: The hour hand sits on the hour wheel, a tube that rides loosely around the cannon pinion. A small set of gears called the motion works takes the minute hand's speed down twelve times, usually in two steps through an intermediate minute wheel. The hour wheel also drives the date mechanism.
details.madeOf: Steel or brass like the minute hand, usually shorter and wider so you can tell them apart at a glance.

parts.name: Hour hand

parts.description: Applied polished index, one for each hour.

details.didYouKnow: Early glow-in-the-dark dials used radioactive radium paint. Today's lume is a non-radioactive pigment that soaks up light and slowly re-emits it.
details.howItWorks: Applied markers are small solid pieces fixed to the dial at each hour position. Tiny feet on their backs push through holes in the dial and are secured from behind. Their polished faces catch light from different angles, making the time easy to read without numbers.
details.madeOf: Usually brass or steel, cut and then diamond-polished, sometimes plated or filled with a strip of luminous pigment such as strontium aluminate.

parts.name: Hour marker

parts.description: Lacquered brass disc; two small feet on its back locate it on the movement.

details.didYouKnow: Dial text is applied by pad printing: a squishy silicone pad lifts ink from an etched plate and presses it onto the dial, letting lettering only a fraction of a millimetre tall come out crisp.
details.howItWorks: The dial is the face you read the time from. Feet on its back slot into holes in the main plate and are clamped by small screws, so it sits precisely around the hand arbors. A window cut in it lets you see the date ring underneath.
details.madeOf: A thin brass disc, finished with lacquer, galvanic plating or a brushed sunburst, then printed with fine text using a soft silicone pad.

parts.name: Dial

parts.description: Ring printed 1 to 31 that a finger flicks forward one step at midnight.

details.didYouKnow: On many watches you should not set the date between roughly 9 pm and 3 am, because the date finger is already engaged and forcing it can damage the teeth.
details.howItWorks: The date ring sits just under the dial with 31 internal teeth. A finger on a wheel that turns once a day, driven by the hour wheel, catches a tooth around midnight and pushes it on by one, and a small sprung jumper snaps it neatly into place. Pulling the crown out one click lets you quickly step it forward by hand.
keyNumbers: Manual corrections: about 5 times a year for short months
details.madeOf: A thin printed ring of metal or plastic, kept as light as possible so the small date finger can move it without stealing much power.

parts.name: Date ring

parts.description: Hour wheel, minute wheel and cannon pinion under the dial: they gear the hour hand down to one turn in twelve hours.

details.didYouKnow: The same 12 to 1 motion works go back to clocks of the 1600s, and most watches still use almost exactly that layout today.
details.howItWorks: The motion works sit under the dial and turn one hand speed into two. The cannon pinion rides on the centre wheel's arbor and turns once an hour, carrying the minute hand. It drives the minute wheel, whose small pinion drives the big hour wheel, and the two steps together slow the hour hand to one turn in twelve hours. The cannon pinion is a friction fit, so when you set the time the hands can turn without dragging the whole gear train with them.
keyNumbers: Hand-setting slip: a friction fit in the cannon pinion
details.madeOf: Brass wheels and hardened steel pinions, cut on small gear-hobbing machines and often left plain because the dial hides them.

parts.name: Motion works

parts.description: Brass foundation of the movement: every wheel pivots in a jewel set into it or into a bridge.

details.didYouKnow: Watchmakers still measure movements in lignes, an old French unit of about 2.26 mm, so a common 11.5 ligne movement is about 26 mm across.
details.howItWorks: The main plate is the base of the movement. The wheels sit between it and the bridges above, with each pivot running in a jewel pressed into one or the other. Holes, recesses and threaded posts are machined into it so every part lines up to within a few thousandths of a millimetre.
keyNumbers: Machining tolerance: often a few microns
details.madeOf: Brass, which machines cleanly and does not rust, usually plated with nickel or rhodium for a bright, stable finish and often decorated with tiny overlapping circles called perlage.

parts.name: Main plate

parts.description: Synthetic ruby bearing; hard and slick, so the steel pivots barely wear.

details.didYouKnow: Jewel bearings were patented in England in 1704, but they only became cheap after a French chemist found a way to grow synthetic rubies around 1900.
details.howItWorks: A jewel bearing is a tiny ruby with a polished hole that a steel pivot turns in. Ruby is so hard and smooth that friction stays low and the hole barely wears, even after billions of turns. A drop of special oil sits in a little cup on the jewel and is held there by surface tension.
keyNumbers: Jewels in a typical automatic: about 21 to 25
details.madeOf: Synthetic ruby, which is lab-grown aluminium oxide with a trace of chromium. It is cheap to make, so jewels add durability rather than value.

parts.name: Jewel bearing

parts.description: Toothed rim of the barrel; it turns slowly as the spring unwinds and drives the whole train.

details.didYouKnow: Watch gears do not use the involute tooth shape found in car gearboxes. They use curves borrowed from cycloids, which work better with the tiny pinions that watches need.
details.howItWorks: The teeth around the barrel mesh with the pinion of the centre wheel. As the mainspring inside slowly unwinds, it turns the whole barrel, and these teeth hand that torque on to the rest of the gear train. They carry the highest force and turn the slowest of any wheel in the train.
keyNumbers: Speed: only a handful of turns per day
Ratio down to the escape wheel: several thousand to one
Torque: highest in the whole train
details.madeOf: Brass or a hard copper alloy, with teeth cut on a gear-hobbing machine so they mesh smoothly with the steel pinion.

parts.name: Barrel teeth

parts.description: Drum holding the mainspring — the watch's fuel tank, good for about two days.

details.didYouKnow: Because the spring slips inside the barrel when full, you can wind an automatic by hand as long as you like without breaking anything.
details.howItWorks: The barrel is a closed drum with the mainspring coiled inside. The spring's inner end hooks onto the central arbor, which winding turns, and its outer end presses against the drum wall, so the drum is pulled round as the spring lets go. In an automatic, the outer end is a sliding bridle that slips when fully wound, so the rotor can never overwind it.
keyNumbers: Parts: drum, lid, arbor and spring
details.madeOf: Brass or a copper-beryllium alloy for the drum and lid, with a hardened steel arbor running through the middle.

parts.name: Mainspring barrel

parts.description: Half a metre of coiled alloy ribbon; its slow unwinding powers everything.

details.didYouKnow: Taken out of its barrel, a modern mainspring relaxes into a curled S shape rather than a flat spiral, a form chosen to give more even force.
details.howItWorks: The mainspring stores the energy that runs the watch. Winding coils it tightly around the barrel arbor, and it slowly uncoils towards the barrel wall, turning the barrel as it goes. Its shape is designed so the force it gives stays fairly even over most of its run, which helps the watch keep steady time.
details.madeOf: Modern springs use a cobalt-nickel alloy such as Nivaflex, which does not rust, resists fatigue and is almost unbreakable. Older ones were blued carbon steel and could snap.

parts.name: Mainspring

parts.description: Turns once an hour; its arbor carries the minute hand up through the dial.

details.didYouKnow: The 60 to 1 step from the centre wheel to the seconds wheel is split across two gear meshes, because one gear 60 times bigger than its pinion would never fit in a watch.
details.howItWorks: The centre wheel is driven by the barrel and turns exactly once an hour. Its arbor pokes up through the dial, where the cannon pinion and minute hand sit on it. It also drives the third wheel, passing power on towards the escapement.
details.madeOf: A brass or copper alloy wheel riveted to a hardened steel pinion, a pairing that wears well because the soft wheel and hard pinion do not gall.

parts.name: Centre wheel

parts.description: Steps the speed up between the centre wheel and the seconds wheel.

details.didYouKnow: Watch wheels are spoked, often with fancy shapes, not just for looks: less mass means less energy wasted in starting and stopping 8 times a second.
details.howItWorks: The third wheel sits between the centre wheel and the fourth wheel. It shares out the 60 to 1 speed-up between two smaller steps, turning faster than the centre wheel but slower than the seconds wheel. Its pivots run in jewels in the main plate and train bridge.
keyNumbers: Speed: roughly once every 7 to 8 minutes
Speed-up per step: about 7 to 8 times
Wheel thickness: a few tenths of a millimetre
details.madeOf: A thin brass wheel with spokes cut away to save weight, riveted onto a polished, hardened steel pinion.

parts.name: Third wheel

parts.description: Turns once a minute; the seconds hand rides on it.

details.didYouKnow: In many watches the seconds hand sits off in a small sub-dial, because putting the fourth wheel at the centre of the movement takes extra gears.
details.howItWorks: The fourth wheel turns once a minute, so its arbor is the natural place for the seconds hand. It drives the escape wheel pinion, which runs much faster still. Every tick of the escapement lets it move forward a tiny step, which is why the seconds hand creeps round in small jumps.
keyNumbers: Ratio to escape wheel: about 16 to 1 at 4 Hz
details.madeOf: Brass wheel on a hardened steel pinion, with a long, slender arbor when it has to reach up through the dial to carry the seconds hand.

parts.name: Fourth (seconds) wheel

parts.description: Hook-toothed wheel that the pallet fork catches and releases, one tooth per tick.

details.didYouKnow: In a Swiss lever escapement the teeth have a club-shaped tip, shaped so the impulse is shared between the tooth and the pallet stone.
details.howItWorks: The escape wheel is the last wheel of the train, always being pushed round by the mainspring's force. The pallet fork lets it advance just a little at each swing of the balance, and as each tooth slides off a pallet stone it pushes back, giving the balance a small kick. In this way it both counts the swings and keeps the balance going.
keyNumbers: Speed: about 16 turns per minute at 4 Hz
details.madeOf: Hardened and polished steel, because its teeth rub against ruby pallets thousands of times a minute. Some modern watches use etched silicon, which needs no oil.

parts.name: Escape wheel

parts.description: Rocking lever with two ruby pallets; it locks the escape wheel and gives the balance a nudge each swing. This is the tick.

details.didYouKnow: The lever escapement was invented by the English watchmaker Thomas Mudge in the 1750s, and almost every mechanical watch made today still uses a version of it.
details.howItWorks: The pallet fork rocks to and fro on its own pivot. As the balance swings past, a ruby pin on it knocks the fork over, which unlocks the escape wheel for an instant; the wheel's tooth then slides across a pallet stone and pushes the fork, which passes that push back to the balance. The other pallet then locks the next tooth, and the sound of each lock is the tick you hear.
details.madeOf: Hardened steel body with two synthetic ruby pallet stones set into it, because the stones must be harder and slicker than the steel escape wheel teeth.

parts.name: Pallet fork

parts.description: The timekeeper: swings back and forth four times a second, like a tiny pendulum.

details.didYouKnow: A watch that is 10 seconds a day out is accurate to about one part in ten thousand, all thanks to a wheel smaller than a fingernail.
details.howItWorks: The balance wheel swings one way, is pulled back by the hairspring, then swings the other way, at a steady rate set by its weight and the spring's stiffness. Each swing lets the pallet fork release the escape wheel once, so the balance decides how fast the whole gear train is allowed to run. A good balance swings through most of a full circle each way.
details.madeOf: Usually Glucydur, a beryllium-copper alloy that is hard, non-magnetic and changes size very little with temperature, so the rate stays stable.

parts.name: Balance wheel

parts.description: Arms joining the rim to the balance staff.

details.didYouKnow: The balance staff pivots are so thin that a hard knock could snap them, which is why most watches mount the balance jewels in spring-loaded shock settings.
details.howItWorks: The spokes link the balance rim to its staff, the axle at the centre. Keeping them thin puts most of the mass at the rim, where it gives the most inertia for the least weight. The staff carries the hairspring collet above and the roller with its impulse jewel below.
keyNumbers: Staff pivots: roughly a tenth of a millimetre across
Arm thickness: a few tenths of a millimetre
details.madeOf: Cut from the same piece of Glucydur as the rim, so rim and arms stay perfectly true, with a hardened steel staff riveted through the centre.

parts.name: Balance spokes

parts.description: Spiral spring finer than a hair; its stiffness sets how fast the balance swings, and so the watch's rate.

details.didYouKnow: The name Nivarox comes from French for neither variable nor oxidising. The balance spring itself was introduced by Christiaan Huygens in 1675 and made pocket watches accurate for the first time.
details.howItWorks: The hairspring's inner end is fixed to the balance staff and its outer end to a stud on the balance cock. As the balance turns, the spring winds or unwinds and pulls it back, so the pair swing like a pendulum. Change the spring's working length or stiffness and the watch runs faster or slower.
keyNumbers: Thickness: a few hundredths of a millimetre
Rate error to keep: usually within about 10 seconds a day
details.madeOf: A special iron-nickel alloy such as Nivarox, which keeps nearly the same stiffness as temperature changes and resists magnetism. Some modern watches use silicon instead.

parts.name: Hairspring

parts.description: Plate that holds the barrel and centre wheel in place from below.

details.didYouKnow: The decoration on bridges is often hidden under the dial or rotor, yet makers still finish it carefully, partly as a mark of quality.
details.howItWorks: The barrel bridge holds the barrel arbor in place, closing the sandwich between it and the main plate. It often carries the winding wheels that take power from the crown and rotor down to the barrel. Steel dowel pins locate it so it goes back in exactly the same spot after every service.
details.madeOf: Real movements usually use brass plated with rhodium or nickel, often decorated with stripes called Côtes de Genève. Plating keeps the brass from tarnishing.

parts.name: Barrel bridge

parts.description: Bridge carrying the lower jewels of the third, fourth and escape wheels.

details.didYouKnow: Jewels are pressed into bridges with a special tool that sets their height to within a few thousandths of a millimetre, which is how endshake is adjusted.
details.howItWorks: The train bridge holds the other end of the third, fourth and escape wheel pivots, each in its own jewel. The gap between bridge and plate is set so each wheel has a tiny amount of up-and-down play, called endshake, letting it spin freely with oil in place. Too little play and the wheels bind; too much and they wobble.
keyNumbers: Endshake per wheel: a few hundredths of a millimetre
Jewels set into it: typically 3 or more
details.madeOf: Plated brass, machined flat and true, with jewels pressed into reamed holes to a precise depth.

parts.name: Train bridge

parts.description: Small bridge carrying the pallet fork's upper pivot in its own jewel.

details.didYouKnow: Watchmakers adjust how deeply the pallets catch the escape wheel in tiny fractions of a millimetre, and that setting has a big effect on how reliably the watch keeps ticking.
details.howItWorks: The pallet fork needs its own small bridge because it sits at a different spot and height from the train wheels. This bridge holds the upper jewel for the fork's arbor, so the fork can rock freely back and forth several times a second. Its exact position matters: move it slightly and the pallets lock deeper or shallower into the escape wheel teeth.
keyNumbers: Fork swing it allows: only a few degrees
details.madeOf: Plated brass like the other bridges, often with the same striped decoration, and a single jewel pressed into it.

parts.name: Pallet bridge

parts.description: Single-armed bridge over the balance; it carries the regulator used to adjust the rate.

details.didYouKnow: Old pocket watch cocks were often hand-engraved with flowers and scrolls, because the balance was the one part owners loved to look at.
details.howItWorks: The balance cock is a bridge held at only one end, so the balance can be fitted and adjusted easily. It carries the upper balance jewel, the stud that holds the hairspring's outer end, and the regulator. Moving the regulator slides two tiny pins along the hairspring, changing its effective length and so the rate.
keyNumbers: Regulator adjustment: a few seconds a day per small nudge
Jewels: usually 2, a hole jewel and a cap jewel
details.madeOf: Plated brass, often with extra decoration since it is the most visible bridge through a display back. The shock setting in it uses a small steel spring.

parts.name: Balance cock

parts.description: Heat-blued steel screw.

details.didYouKnow: Watchmakers judge bluing by eye, watching the steel run from straw to brown to purple to blue and stopping at exactly the right moment.
details.howItWorks: Bridge screws clamp the bridges down onto the main plate, holding every wheel at the right height. They thread into the plate and seat firmly on the bridge surface. They must be tight enough to stay put but not so tight that the soft brass threads strip.
keyNumbers: Thread size: often around 1 mm or less
Shown as separate parts here: 5, with a few more riding on their bridges
details.madeOf: Steel, heated until a thin oxide layer forms on the surface and gives it a deep blue colour. The colour comes from that film, not from paint.

parts.name: Bridge screw

parts.description: Big toothed wheel on the barrel arbor, held by a sprung click so winding can't slip back.

details.didYouKnow: The faint clicking you feel when you wind a watch by hand is this pawl riding over the ratchet teeth one by one.
details.howItWorks: The ratchet wheel sits square on the barrel arbor, so turning it winds the mainspring. Power arrives from the crown through the crown wheel beside it, or from the rotor through a train of reduction wheels. A small sprung pawl called the click drops into its teeth, so the wheel can turn one way to wind but can't run back. Without it, the mainspring would unwind straight back through the crown the moment you let go.
keyNumbers: Click: usually a single pawl with its own spring
Visible through a display back: usually yes
details.madeOf: Hardened steel, usually with a decorative circular graining or sunburst finish, held on by a large flat screw that often has a left-hand thread.

parts.name: Ratchet wheel & click

parts.description: Ball bearing the rotor spins on.

details.didYouKnow: A worn rotor bearing lets the rotor tilt and scrape the inside of the case back, and the scratching sound is a common sign a watch needs a service.
details.howItWorks: The rotor bearing lets the heavy rotor spin with very little friction in either direction. It is a tiny ring of balls running between an inner and outer race, fixed to the centre of the movement. A winding wheel underneath picks up the rotor's motion and sends it down to the barrel through reverser wheels.
keyNumbers: Ball diameter: roughly half a millimetre
details.madeOf: Hardened steel races and balls, or sometimes ceramic balls, which are lighter and need no oil. Some makers use a ruby jewel bearing instead.

parts.name: Rotor bearing

parts.description: Heavy half-disc that swings with every move of your wrist and winds the mainspring.

details.didYouKnow: If you sit very still all day, an automatic can slowly run down. Most need several hours of normal wear a day to stay fully wound.
details.howItWorks: The rotor is an off-centre weight that gravity keeps pointing downwards, so every move of your wrist makes the movement turn around it. That swinging is geared down heavily and used to wind the mainspring a little at a time. Reverser wheels let it wind whichever way it spins.
keyNumbers: Swing: free through a full 360 degrees
Gear reduction to barrel: very high, often over 100 to 1
details.madeOf: Steel or brass, often with a heavy rim of tungsten alloy, which is very dense and so packs more swing into a small space. Luxury watches sometimes use solid gold.

parts.name: Winding rotor

summary: An automatic wristwatch with no battery: a coiled mainspring, wound by the swinging rotor as you move, drives a train of gears that the balance wheel releases one tick at a time, about eight ticks a second.
